<script type="application/json" id="pack-y3w03">{"year":3,"week":3,"id":"y3w03","title":"Logical Reasoning III: Investigating Real-Life Problems","subtitle":"Testing everyday claims with evidence; the investigation cycle and Pólya’s problem-solving steps; designing fair survey questions and samples; analysing data with averages, percentages and rates; avoiding common errors such as generalising from a few cases or confusing association with cause; and using costs, savings and break-even points to decide on school and community problems.","family":"number","section":{"no":1,"name":"Logical Reasoning and Variation","strand":"Number for Everyday Life","from":1,"to":5},"outcomes":["Distinguish a claim from the evidence for it, and test claims from peers logically.","Plan and carry out a mini-investigation using the investigation cycle.","Write fair, clear survey questions and choose a sample that avoids bias.","Analyse data with averages, percentages and rates, and draw valid conclusions.","Recognise invalid conclusions: over-generalisation, majority versus most popular, and association versus cause.","Use cost, saving and break-even calculations to justify decisions on real school and community problems."],"keywords":["claim","evidence","investigation","objective","survey","interview","observation","sample","bias","leading question","mean","median","mode","percentage","majority","association","causation","cost-benefit","break-even","payback period","Pólya"],"notes":[{"title":"Claims and evidence","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"In arguments among peers, the person who shouts loudest sometimes “wins”, even without the most valid points. Logical reasoning replaces volume with **evidence**."},{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Claim, evidence and conclusion","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["A **claim** is a statement someone wants us to accept: “The mathematics teacher always comes to class.”","**Evidence** is information that can be checked: attendance records, measurements, survey results.","A **conclusion** is **valid** when the evidence supports it, and **not valid** when the evidence is missing, too small, biased, or points elsewhere."]}]},{"k":"p","text":"Words such as **always**, **never**, **every** and **all** make a claim strong, and one counterexample destroys it. Words such as **usually**, **most** and **tends to** make a weaker claim that needs proportions to test."},{"k":"p","text":"Everyday questions that can be investigated include: *Will the mathematics teacher come to class today? Which school will win the next National Science and Maths Quiz? Can Ghana ever win the World Cup?* Some have answers supported by long records; others can only be judged as likely or unlikely."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"The investigation cycle","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w03-cycle","caption":"Problem, plan, analyse, conclude, then look back."},{"k":"ol","items":["**Identify the objective**: what exactly are we trying to find out?","**Gather data** by interview, survey, observation, measurement or records.","**Analyse the data** with tables, charts, averages and percentages to find patterns.","**Conclude on the argument**: is the claim valid? What are the limits of the evidence?"]},{"k":"p","text":"The mathematician **George Pólya** described the same idea as four steps for solving any problem: **understand the problem, devise a plan, carry out the plan, and look back**."}],"figs":["w03-cycle"]},{"title":"Collecting good data","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Poor survey questions","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Leading**: “Don’t you agree that the canteen food is too expensive?” pushes the answer.","**Double-barrelled**: “Is the food tasty and cheap?” asks two things at once.","**Vague**: “Do you use water often?” — what is “often”?","**Unanswerable or sensitive**: questions people cannot or will not answer honestly."]},{"k":"p","text":"A good question is short, neutral, asks one thing, and offers clear options: “How many times did you buy food at the canteen last week? 0 / 1–2 / 3–4 / 5 or more.”"}]},{"k":"p","text":"A **sample** is the group we actually ask. It must represent the whole **population**:"},{"k":"ul","items":["**Bias** occurs when some groups are left out or over-represented (asking only boarders about a day-student problem).","A **larger** sample gives more reliable results than a tiny one.","**Random** selection (picking names from a box) gives every member a fair chance."]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Analysing and concluding","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Useful measures","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["mean $=\\dfrac{\\text{sum of values}}{\\text{number of values}}$; median = middle value in order; mode = most common value","percentage $=\\dfrac{\\text{part}}{\\text{whole}}\\times100\\%$","rate, for example litres per day or cost per kWh","energy (kWh) $=\\dfrac{\\text{power (W)}\\times\\text{hours}}{1000}$"]}]},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Valid and invalid conclusions","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["A **majority** means **more than 50%**. The most popular choice is not necessarily a majority.","An average does not describe every individual: a mean age of 17 does not mean everyone is 17.","A pattern in a **sample** describes the population only if the sample is fair.","**Association is not causation**: if two quantities rise or fall together, a third factor may cause both.","$p\\Rightarrow q$ and $q$ true does **not** give $p$ (affirming the consequent, Week 2)."]}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Deciding with numbers","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Many school and community problems are decisions between options. Compare them with:"},{"k":"ul","items":["**total cost** = initial cost + running cost $\\times$ time;","**saving** = old cost $-$ new cost;","**break-even point**: the time at which two options cost the same;","**payback period** = $\\dfrac{\\text{cost of the change}}{\\text{saving per unit time}}$."]},{"k":"p","text":"Then weigh the factors that numbers do not capture: safety, convenience, fairness and the environment."},{"k":"box","kind":"life","title":"Investigations in your community","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Optimising water and electricity use in school, choosing between grass and stones to control erosion, deciding where to place a borehole, planning provisions for a term, or testing a rumour before sharing it: each is a mini-investigation with an objective, data, analysis and a justified conclusion."}]}],"figs":[]}],"examples":[{"title":"Is the prefect always first?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A student claims: “The class prefect is always the first to come to class, so the prefect was the first to come to class today.” Records for ten school days show who arrived first: the prefect on 7 days, Akosua on 2 days and Yaw on 1 day. (a) Is the general claim true? (b) Is the conclusion about today valid? (c) What evidence would settle it?"}],"steps":["(a) “Always” is contradicted by 3 of the 10 days: the claim is **false**. The data support “the prefect is **usually** first” ($\\tfrac{7}{10}=70\\%$ of days).","(b) The conclusion rests on a false premise, so it is **not valid**. It may still happen to be true; we cannot tell from the argument.","(c) Today’s own evidence: the register, a classmate who arrived early, or the time the classroom was opened."],"answer":"(a) false (b) not valid (c) evidence about today itself","figs":["w03-arrivals"]},{"title":"Are all SHS 3 students 17?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"“SHS 3 students are expected to be 17 years old. We are in SHS 3, so every member is 17.” Twelve students give their ages: 17, 20, 18, 16, 16, 17, 17, 18, 16, 16, 17, 18. (a) Find the mean, median and mode. (b) Test the claim. (c) What valid conclusion can be drawn?"}],"steps":["(a) Sum $=206$, so mean $=\\dfrac{206}{12}\\approx17.17$ years.","In order: 16, 16, 16, 16, 17, 17, 17, 17, 18, 18, 18, 20. Median $=\\dfrac{17+17}{2}=17$. Modes: 16 and 17 (four each).","(b) Only 4 of the 12 students ($33\\tfrac13\\%$) are 17, so “every member is 17” is **false**; the counterexamples include the four 16-year-olds and the 20-year-old.","(c) Valid: “The **typical** age of the class is about 17 years; ages range from 16 to 20.” An expected (average) value does not describe each person."],"answer":"(a) mean ≈ 17.17, median 17, modes 16 and 17 (b) false (c) the typical age is about 17","figs":["w03-ages"]},{"title":"From weak subjects to failing","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Claim: “If a student failed mathematics last term, then mathematics needs improvement. Mathematics and Science need improvement for Efua, so Efua failed mathematics last term.” Efua’s scores last term were Mathematics 52, Science 48, English 74 and Social Studies 81, with a pass mark of 40. Is the conclusion valid?"}],"steps":["Write $p$: Efua failed mathematics; $q$: mathematics needs improvement. The premise is $p\\Rightarrow q$ and we are told $q$.","Concluding $p$ from $p\\Rightarrow q$ and $q$ is **affirming the consequent**: invalid in form.","The evidence agrees: Efua scored 52, above the pass mark of 40, so she **passed**.","Mathematics needs improvement because it is one of her weaker subjects compared with English (74) and Social Studies (81), not because she failed."],"answer":"Not valid: she passed with 52; “needs improvement” does not imply “failed”.","figs":[]},{"title":"Planning an investigation","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Many students arrive late on Monday mornings. Plan an investigation into the claim “Students are late mainly because of transport problems.”"}],"steps":["**Objective:** find the main causes of Monday lateness and test whether transport is the main one.","**Data:** for four Mondays, record every late student’s arrival time; give each a short questionnaire with one question “What was the main reason you were late?” and options: transport, chores at home, woke up late, distance, other.","**Sample:** all late students (not only one class), to avoid bias.","**Analysis:** tally the reasons, convert to percentages, and draw a bar chart; compare the mean lateness (minutes) for each reason.","**Conclusion:** the claim is supported only if transport is given by **more than half** of late students; if transport is merely the largest group, say “the most common single cause”.","**Look back:** suggest actions (an earlier bus, a chores timetable) and re-measure."],"answer":"Objective → questionnaire and records for four Mondays → tally, percentages, chart → valid conclusion → act and re-measure.","figs":[]},{"title":"Improving survey questions","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Explain what is wrong with each question and rewrite it. (a) “Don’t you think the school should stop wasting water?” (b) “Is the library quiet and well stocked?” (c) “Do you use electricity a lot?”"}],"steps":["(a) **Leading**: it suggests the answer. Better: “Which of these do you think uses the most water in school? Washing / bathing / cooking / leaking taps / other.”","(b) **Double-barrelled**: a student may find the library quiet but poorly stocked. Better: two questions, “How quiet is the library? (1–5)” and “How often do you find the book you need? Never / sometimes / usually / always.”","(c) **Vague**: “a lot” means different things. Better: “For how many hours a day are the lights in your classroom on? 0–2 / 3–5 / 6–8 / more than 8.”"],"answer":"(a) leading (b) double-barrelled (c) vague; rewrite each as a neutral, single, measurable question.","figs":[]},{"title":"A biased sample","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"To decide whether the canteen should open at 6:30 a.m., the canteen manager asks 40 boarding students; 35 say yes. She concludes “87.5% of the school want the canteen to open at 6:30 a.m.” The school has 600 boarders and 900 day students. Is her conclusion valid? How should the survey be done?"}],"steps":["$\\dfrac{35}{40}=87.5\\%$ of the **sample** said yes.","Day students, who are $\\dfrac{900}{1500}=60\\%$ of the school and mostly arrive after 6:30 a.m., were not asked at all. The sample is **biased**.","So the conclusion about “the school” is **not valid**; it may describe boarders only.","Better: choose a random sample in proportion, for example 40 boarders and 60 day students out of 100, and report the two groups separately."],"answer":"Not valid (biased sample); use a proportional random sample of boarders and day students.","figs":[]},{"title":"Most students or most popular?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"In a survey of 80 students, 34 chose jollof as their favourite dish, 26 chose waakye and 20 chose banku. (a) Draw a pie chart. (b) A student claims “Most students prefer jollof.” Is this valid? (c) Write a valid conclusion."}],"steps":["(a) Angles: jollof $\\dfrac{34}{80}\\times360^\\circ=153^\\circ$, waakye $\\dfrac{26}{80}\\times360^\\circ=117^\\circ$, banku $\\dfrac{20}{80}\\times360^\\circ=90^\\circ$. Check: $153+117+90=360$ ✓.","(b) Jollof: $\\dfrac{34}{80}\\times100\\%=42.5\\%$. “Most students” means more than 50%, so the claim is **not valid**: 57.5% preferred something else.","(c) “Jollof is the **most popular** single dish, chosen by 42.5% of the students surveyed.”"],"answer":"(b) not valid: 42.5% is not a majority (c) jollof is the most popular choice","figs":["w03-food"]},{"title":"Phones and test scores","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Data from ten students (daily hours of phone use, test score %): (0.5, 78), (1, 74), (1.5, 70), (2, 72), (2.5, 63), (3, 60), (3.5, 61), (4, 52), (4.5, 55), (5, 48). (a) Describe the relationship. (b) Does the data prove that phone use causes low scores? (c) How could the claim be tested more fairly?"}],"steps":["(a) The points fall from left to right (Figure 3.5): there is a **negative association**. Each extra hour goes with about 6 marks less on average.","(b) No. Association is not causation. A third factor could explain both, such as the time spent studying, sleep, or interest in the subject. Phones can also be used for learning.","(c) Collect data on study time and sleep as well, compare students with **similar** study time, or run a fair trial in which one group limits phone use for a month while a similar group does not, then compare score changes."],"answer":"(a) negative association (b) no (c) control other factors or run a fair trial","figs":["w03-phones"]},{"title":"Lab upgrade or tablets?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A school has a grant of GH₵20 000. Option A: repair and upgrade 20 lab computers at GH₵1000 each; the lab is open 30 one-hour periods a week for all 1200 students. Option B: buy tablets at GH₵1250 each for the mathematics department, used in 35 one-hour mathematics periods a week, shared by the same 1200 students. (a) Find the number of tablets. (b) Compare device-minutes per student per week. (c) Give two other factors and make a justified recommendation."}],"steps":["(a) $20\\,000\\div1250=16$ tablets.","(b) A: $20\\times30\\times60=36\\,000$ device-minutes a week; per student $36\\,000\\div1200=30$ minutes.","B: $16\\times35\\times60=33\\,600$ device-minutes; per student $33\\,600\\div1200=28$ minutes.","On access alone the options are almost equal (30 against 28 minutes).","(c) Tablets are portable (field trips, any classroom) and keep working through power cuts on battery; lab computers have larger screens for typing and programming and are harder to steal or break.","Recommendation (one valid answer): if power cuts are frequent, choose tablets, since lab time is lost whenever the power goes off; otherwise the lab serves all subjects equally."],"answer":"(a) 16 (b) 30 min against 28 min (c) a justified choice weighing portability and power cuts against screen size and security","figs":["w03-tech"]},{"title":"Saving electricity","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Forty classroom tubes of 36 W are left on for 4 hours a day after classes. Electricity costs GH₵1.80 per kWh and a term has 65 school days. (a) Find the cost per term of leaving them on. (b) Find the saving if they are switched off. (c) If they are replaced with 18 W LED tubes but still left on, find the cost per term. (d) Each LED tube costs GH₵45. After how many terms does the replacement pay for itself (ignore the switch-off option)?"}],"steps":["(a) Power: $40\\times36=1440$ W. Energy per day: $\\dfrac{1440\\times4}{1000}=5.76$ kWh.","Cost per day: $5.76\\times1.80=10.368$; per term: $10.368\\times65=673.92$, that is GH₵673.92.","(b) Switching off saves the whole GH₵673.92 per term.","(c) Half the power, so half the cost: GH₵336.96.","(d) Cost of tubes: $40\\times45=1800$. The LEDs save $673.92-336.96=336.96$ per term on these hours alone. Payback $=\\dfrac{1800}{336.96}\\approx5.3$ terms (they also save during class hours, so in practice it is faster)."],"answer":"(a) GH₵673.92 (b) GH₵673.92 (c) GH₵336.96 (d) about 5.3 terms","figs":["w03-energy"]},{"title":"Dripping taps","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A dripping tap loses 1 drop per second, and 20 drops make 1 millilitre. A school has 15 dripping taps. Water costs GH₵12 per cubic metre ($1\\text{ m}^3=1000$ litres). (a) How many litres are lost per tap per day? (b) Find the volume lost by all 15 taps in a year. (c) Find the yearly cost. (d) Repairing a tap costs GH₵5. Find the payback period in months."}],"steps":["(a) Drops per day: $60\\times60\\times24=86\\,400$. Volume: $86\\,400\\div20=4320$ mL $=4.32$ litres.","(b) $15\\times4.32=64.8$ litres a day; $64.8\\times365=23\\,652$ litres $=23.652\\text{ m}^3$.","(c) $23.652\\times12\\approx283.82$, that is about GH₵283.82 a year.","(d) Repairs: $15\\times5=75$. Saving per month: $283.82\\div12\\approx23.65$. Payback $=75\\div23.65\\approx3.2$ months."],"answer":"(a) 4.32 L (b) 23 652 L (c) about GH₵283.82 (d) about 3.2 months","figs":[]},{"title":"Grass or stones?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A slope of 120 m² in your community is being eroded. Grass costs GH₵8 per m² to plant and GH₵240 a year to maintain. Stone pitching costs GH₵25 per m² to lay and GH₵30 a year to maintain. (a) Write the total cost $C$ after $t$ years for each. (b) Find the break-even time. (c) Which is better for 5 years? For 15 years? (d) Give one non-cost factor."}],"steps":["(a) Grass: $C=120\\times8+240t=960+240t$. Stones: $C=120\\times25+30t=3000+30t$.","(b) $960+240t=3000+30t$ gives $210t=2040$, so $t=\\dfrac{2040}{210}\\approx9.7$ years.","(c) 5 years: grass $960+1200=2160$; stones $3000+150=3150$. **Grass** is cheaper.","15 years: grass $960+3600=4560$; stones $3000+450=3450$. **Stones** are cheaper.","(d) Grass needs water and time to take root, so it may fail on a steep slope in the first heavy rains; stones work at once but heat up and give no habitat."],"answer":"(a) $960+240t$; $3000+30t$ (b) about 9.7 years (c) grass for 5 years, stones for 15 years","figs":["w03-erosion"]},{"title":"The empty food box","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Kwesi’s food box is empty, and he has GH₵450 for a 13-week term. Each week he needs gari and sugar costing GH₵18 and milk costing GH₵8. He must also buy soap and toiletries once, for GH₵40. Use Pólya’s four steps to decide how much he can spend on extras each week."}],"steps":["**Understand:** total money GH₵450; fixed weekly costs; a one-off cost; find the weekly amount left for extras.","**Plan:** total essential cost $=13\\times(\\text{weekly cost})+\\text{one-off cost}$, then share what remains over 13 weeks.","**Carry out:** weekly essentials $18+8=26$; term essentials $13\\times26=338$; plus $40$ gives $378$.","Money left: $450-378=72$. Per week: $72\\div13\\approx5.54$, so GH₵5.50 a week (rounding down so that he does not run short).","**Look back:** $378+13\\times5.50=449.50\\le450$ ✓. If prices rise by 10%, essentials become $415.80$ and he would have only about GH₵2.63 a week, so he should keep a reserve."],"answer":"About GH₵5.50 a week for extras","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results","items":["Test a claim with evidence; “always/every” is destroyed by one counterexample.","Investigation cycle: objective → data → analysis → conclusion → look back (Pólya: understand, plan, carry out, look back).","Good questions are neutral, single and measurable; samples must be fair and large enough.","A majority is more than 50%; an average does not describe every individual.","Association is not causation.","Total cost = initial + running × time; break-even where the costs are equal; payback = cost ÷ saving per unit time."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"Which word makes a claim that a single counterexample destroys?","options":["always","usually","often","tends to"],"correct":0,"explain":"“Always” allows no exceptions."},{"q":"“Wouldn’t you agree that the new timetable is better?” is an example of","options":["a leading question","a double-barrelled question","a random sample","a neutral question"],"correct":0,"explain":"It pushes the respondent towards “yes”."},{"q":"In a survey of 200 students, 90 chose football as their favourite sport. Which conclusion is valid?","options":["Football is the most popular choice, but not a majority.","Most students prefer football.","All students like football.","Football is chosen by a majority of 90%."],"correct":0,"explain":"$90\\div200=45\\%<50\\%$."},{"q":"The mean of 14, 16, 16, 18 and 21 is","options":["17","16","18","16.5"],"correct":0,"explain":"$85\\div5=17$."},{"q":"A study finds that towns with more ice-cream sales have more drowning cases. The most reasonable explanation is","options":["hot weather increases both","ice cream causes drowning","drowning causes ice-cream sales","the data must be wrong"],"correct":0,"explain":"A third factor (heat) drives both."},{"q":"Ten 60 W bulbs are left on for 5 hours. How much energy is used?","options":["3 kWh","30 kWh","0.3 kWh","300 kWh"],"correct":0,"explain":"$\\dfrac{10\\times60\\times5}{1000}=3$ kWh."},{"q":"Option A costs $500+80t$ and option B costs $1100+20t$ after $t$ years. They cost the same when $t=$","options":["10","6","8","12"],"correct":0,"explain":"$60t=600$."},{"q":"A water-saving device costs GH₵240 and saves GH₵30 a month. Its payback period is","options":["8 months","6 months","7.2 months","12 months"],"correct":0,"explain":"$240\\div30=8$."},{"q":"Surveying only students in the science block about the whole school’s lunch preferences gives","options":["a biased sample","a random sample","a census","a valid conclusion about the school"],"correct":0,"explain":"Other groups are left out."},{"q":"The last of Pólya’s four problem-solving steps is","options":["look back","devise a plan","understand the problem","gather data"],"correct":0,"explain":"Check the answer and whether it makes sense."}],"exercise":[{"q":"The claim “It always rains in Kumasi in June” is tested over 30 days of June: it rained on 21. Is the claim true? Write a valid statement.","a":"False; it rained on 70% of June days"},{"q":"Find the mean, median and mode of the ages 15, 16, 16, 17, 17, 17, 18, 19, and decide whether “most students are 17” is valid.","a":"Mean 16.875, median 17, mode 17; 3 of 8 = 37.5%, so not valid"},{"q":"Rewrite the question “Do you agree that girls are better at science than boys?” as a neutral question.","a":"e.g. “What was your score in the last science test?” and compare groups"},{"q":"In a survey of 150 people, 81 support a new market. What percentage is this, and is it a majority?","a":"54%; yes"},{"q":"A sample of 30 Form 1 students is used to judge the study habits of the whole school. Explain the problem and suggest a better sample.","a":"Biased: only one year; sample from every year in proportion"},{"q":"Twenty 40 W fans run for 6 hours a day for 60 days at GH₵1.80 per kWh. Find the cost.","a":"288 kWh; GH₵518.40"},{"q":"A borehole costs GH₵18 000 and saves GH₵1500 a month on water bills. Find the payback period.","a":"12 months"},{"q":"Paint A costs GH₵600 and lasts 3 years; paint B costs GH₵1500 and lasts 8 years. Which is cheaper per year?","a":"A: GH₵200 a year; B: GH₵187.50 a year, so B"},{"q":"Option P costs $2000+150t$ and option Q costs $800+300t$ after $t$ months. Find the break-even time and the cheaper option for one year.","a":"8 months; for 12 months P (3800 against 4400)"},{"q":"“Students who eat breakfast score higher, so breakfast causes higher scores.” Give two other factors that could explain this.","a":"e.g. more organised homes, more sleep, family support"},{"q":"A tap drips 2 drops per second, and 20 drops make 1 mL. How many litres are lost in a 30-day month?","a":"259.2 L"},{"q":"Ama has GH₵300 for 12 weeks. Her fixed weekly spending is GH₵19 and she must buy a GH₵36 book once. How much can she spend on extras per week?","a":"$300-264=36$; GH₵3 a week"}],"theory":[{"q":"“If the computer lab is upgraded, all students will have access, but each student will have limited time.” (a) Use the figures 20 computers, 30 one-hour periods a week and 1200 students to find each student’s weekly time. (b) Give three reasons why the statement is or is not valid. (c) Suggest one way to increase each student’s time without buying computers.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) $20\\times30\\times60=36\\,000$ computer-minutes; $36\\,000\\div1200=30$ minutes per student per week."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) Valid: (1) every student can be timetabled, so “all students will have access” is achievable; (2) 30 minutes a week is short for practical work, so “limited time” is accurate; (3) power cuts or broken computers reduce the time further, which supports “limited”."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) Open the lab after classes and at weekends, or pair students so that two use one computer for group tasks (more students per session)."}]},{"q":"The head of the Agricultural Science department says: “If tablets are bought for the mathematics department, only mathematics students will benefit, and they will have continuous access during mathematics lessons at the expense of my department.” Give three reasons why this view is or is not valid.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(1) Not valid: every SHS student studies Core Mathematics, so all students benefit, including Agricultural Science students."},{"k":"p","text":"(2) Not valid: the tablets can be booked by other departments when mathematics lessons are not running; continuous access is a timetabling choice, not a consequence of the purchase."},{"k":"p","text":"(3) Partly valid: if the mathematics department controls the tablets, other departments may get little use. A fair booking timetable would remove this concern."},{"k":"p","text":"So the conclusion “only mathematics students will benefit” does not follow from the premise."}]},{"q":"There is erosion in your school compound. Plan and describe an investigation to decide between planting grass and laying stones. Include: (a) the objective (b) the stakeholders you will consult and the questions you will ask (c) the data you will measure (d) how you will analyse the data (e) how you will reach a valid conclusion.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) Objective: decide which method, grass or stones, controls erosion on the affected areas at the lowest long-term cost and with acceptable effort."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) Stakeholders: the estate officer, agriculture teacher, groundsmen, a mason, and students who use the paths. Questions: “What did the last repair cost?”, “How long do grass or stones last here?”, “How much water and labour does grass need?”"},{"k":"p","text":"(c) Measure the eroded area (m²), the slope, costs per m² of each method, and yearly maintenance costs."},{"k":"p","text":"(d) Write total cost equations such as $C=960+240t$ and $C=3000+30t$, draw the graphs, find the break-even time and compare costs over the expected period."},{"k":"p","text":"(e) Combine cost with non-cost factors (steepness, water supply, appearance, safety). For example, if the area must be protected for more than 10 years and the slope is steep, conclude that stones are better, stating the assumptions."}]},{"q":"A news report says: “A survey of 50 people at a Kumasi bus station found that 70% think fuel prices will fall next month. So most Ghanaians expect fuel prices to fall.” Evaluate this conclusion using at least four ideas from this week.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(1) Sample size: 50 people is a small sample for a country of more than 30 million."},{"k":"p","text":"(2) Bias: people at one bus station in one city are not representative of all Ghanaians (rural areas, other regions, non-travellers are left out)."},{"k":"p","text":"(3) The percentage: 70% of the sample is a majority of the sample, but this does not transfer to the population when the sample is biased."},{"k":"p","text":"(4) Opinion versus fact: what people expect is not evidence of what will happen; prices depend on world oil prices and exchange rates."},{"k":"p","text":"(5) The question wording is unknown; a leading question could inflate the figure."},{"k":"p","text":"So the conclusion is not valid. A valid statement is: “70% of 50 people asked at one Kumasi bus station expected prices to fall.”"}]},{"q":"A school’s monthly electricity bill is about GH₵4200. Design a plan to cut it by at least 15%. Your plan should (a) say what data you will collect (b) include one calculation of a possible saving, with stated assumptions (c) explain how you will test whether the plan worked.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) Data: the bills for the last six months, the number and wattage of lights, fans and computers in each building, and the hours they are on (by observation over a week)."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) Example: 120 tubes of 36 W are on 3 hours a day longer than needed for 22 days a month at GH₵1.80 per kWh. Energy wasted $=\\dfrac{120\\times36\\times3\\times22}{1000}=285.12$ kWh; cost about GH₵513. Switching them off saves about $513\\div4200\\approx12\\%$. Adding fans switched off when rooms are empty can reach the 15% target."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) Compare the bills for three months after the plan with the same months before, allowing for changes in <script type="application/json" id="pack-y3w04">{"year":3,"week":4,"id":"y3w04","title":"Variation I: Direct, Inverse, Joint and Combined Variation","subtitle":"Proportional reasoning; direct variation, including variation with squares, cubes and roots; inverse variation and inverse-square laws; joint and combined variation; finding and using the constant of variation; recognising variation from tables and straight-line graphs; percentage changes; and the limits of variation models in real life.","family":"number","section":{"no":1,"name":"Logical Reasoning and Variation","strand":"Number for Everyday Life","from":1,"to":5},"outcomes":["Express direct, inverse, joint and combined variation in words, with the symbol $\\propto$, and as equations with a constant $k$.","Find the constant of variation from given data and use the equation to find unknown values.","Decide from a table whether two quantities vary directly or inversely, and with which power.","Recognise variation from graphs and use straight-line plots to confirm it.","Work out the effect of scaling or percentage changes in the variables.","Model real situations with variation and explain when the model may fail."],"keywords":["variation","proportion","constant of variation","direct variation","inverse variation","joint variation","combined variation","square law","inverse-square law","hyperbola","ratio","product","proportional reasoning","scale factor","percentage change","model"],"notes":[{"title":"Variation and proportional reasoning","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"In many real situations a change in one quantity produces a **predictable** change in another: the more bags of rice you buy, the more you pay; the faster a bus travels, the less time the journey takes. Mathematics describes such relationships as **variation**. This week covers direct, inverse, joint and combined variation; Week 5 treats **partial** variation."},{"k":"p","text":"The symbol $\\propto$ means “varies as” or “is proportional to”. Every variation statement becomes an equation by introducing a **constant of variation** $k$ (also called the constant of proportionality)."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Direct variation","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Direct variation","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"$y$ **varies directly** as $x$ if $y=kx$ for a constant $k\\neq0$. We write $y\\propto x$."},{"k":"ul","items":["The **ratio** $\\dfrac{y}{x}=k$ is the same for every pair of values.","Doubling $x$ doubles $y$; multiplying $x$ by any factor multiplies $y$ by the same factor.","The graph of $y$ against $x$ is a **straight line through the origin** with gradient $k$."]}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w04-direct","caption":"Direct variation: straight lines through the origin."},{"k":"p","text":"Examples: the cost of bananas at GH₵5 per kg is $C=5w$; the distance travelled at constant speed $s$ is $d=st$."},{"k":"p","text":"Variation can also be with a **power** or **root**:"},{"k":"table","head":["Statement","Equation","$x$ multiplied by 2 gives $y$ multiplied by"],"rows":[["$y\\propto x^2$","$y=kx^2$","4"],["$y\\propto x^3$","$y=kx^3$","8"],["$y\\propto\\sqrt x$","$y=k\\sqrt x$","$\\sqrt2\\approx1.41$"]]}],"figs":["w04-direct"]},{"title":"Inverse variation","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Inverse variation","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"$y$ **varies inversely** as $x$ if $y=\\dfrac{k}{x}$ for a constant $k\\neq0$. We write $y\\propto\\dfrac1x$."},{"k":"ul","items":["The **product** $xy=k$ is the same for every pair of values.","Doubling $x$ halves $y$; multiplying $x$ by a factor divides $y$ by that factor.","The graph is a **rectangular hyperbola**: it approaches the axes but never meets them."]}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w04-inverse","caption":"Inverse variation: every rectangle under the curve has the same area."},{"k":"p","text":"Examples: the time to finish a job varies inversely as the number of workers; for a fixed distance $d$, time $t=\\dfrac ds$ varies inversely as speed. The **inverse-square** law $y=\\dfrac{k}{x^2}$ describes light intensity, sound intensity and gravitational force: doubling the distance gives **one quarter** of the effect."},{"k":"table","head":["Type","Statement","Equation","Constant quantity"],"rows":[["direct","$y\\propto x$","$y=kx$","$\\dfrac yx=k$"],["inverse","$y\\propto\\dfrac1x$","$y=\\dfrac kx$","$xy=k$"]]}],"figs":["w04-inverse"]},{"title":"Joint and combined variation","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Joint and combined variation","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Joint variation**: $y$ varies jointly as $x$ and $z$ if $y=kxz$. For example, the volume of a cone $V=khr^2$, with $k=\\tfrac{\\pi}{3}$.","**Combined variation**: $y$ varies directly as $x$ and inversely as $z$ if $y=\\dfrac{kx}{z}$. For example, gas pressure $P=\\dfrac{knT}{V}$."]}]},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Method for every variation problem","blocks":[{"k":"ol","items":["Write the statement with $\\propto$, then as an equation with $k$.","Substitute the given set of values and solve for $k$.","Write the equation with the value of $k$.","Substitute the new values to find the unknown, and give units."]}]},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Scaling without finding $k$","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"If $y=\\dfrac{kx^2}{z}$, then $\\dfrac{y_2}{y_1}=\\left(\\dfrac{x_2}{x_1}\\right)^2\\div\\dfrac{z_2}{z_1}$. So if $x$ rises by 10% and $z$ falls by 20%, $y$ is multiplied by $\\dfrac{1.1^2}{0.8}=1.5125$: an increase of 51.25%."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Recognising variation from data","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["If $\\dfrac yx$ is constant, $y\\propto x$; if $\\dfrac{y}{x^2}$ is constant, $y\\propto x^2$.","If $xy$ is constant, $y\\propto\\dfrac1x$; if $x^2y$ is constant, $y\\propto\\dfrac{1}{x^2}$.","On a graph, $y\\propto x^2$ gives a straight line through the origin when $y$ is plotted against $x^2$, and $y\\propto\\dfrac1x$ gives one when $y$ is plotted against $\\dfrac1x$."]},{"k":"fig","id":"w04-tests","caption":"Straight-line tests for variation."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Models have limits","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A variation model is an ideal. The Accra–Kumasi time model $T=\\dfrac{240}{S}$ assumes a constant speed; at festive seasons, traffic, police checks and accidents break that assumption. A model should always be checked against reality and used only within sensible values."}]},{"k":"box","kind":"life","title":"Variation in science and daily life","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Hooke’s law (extension $\\propto$ force), Ohm’s law ($V\\propto I$), Boyle’s law ($P\\propto\\tfrac1V$), the pendulum ($T\\propto\\sqrt L$), stopping distance ($d\\propto v^2$), light intensity ($I\\propto\\tfrac{1}{d^2}$), and costs, wages and rations in the market all follow variation laws."}]}],"figs":["w04-tests"]}],"examples":[{"title":"Bags of rice","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A bag of rice costs GH₵120. The cost $C$ (GH₵) varies directly as the number of bags $n$. (a) Express $C$ in terms of $n$. (b) A customer pays GH₵600. How many bags did she buy? (c) A trader has GH₵2000. What is the greatest number of bags she can buy, and how much change does she get?"}],"steps":["(a) $C\\propto n$, so $C=kn$. When $n=1$, $C=120$: $k=120$, so $C=120n$.","(b) $600=120n$, $n=\\dfrac{600}{120}=5$ bags.","(c) $120n\\le2000$ gives $n\\le16.67$, so 16 bags.","Cost $120\\times16=1920$; change $2000-1920=80$, that is GH₵80."],"answer":"(a) $C=120n$ (b) 5 bags (c) 16 bags, GH₵80 change","figs":[]},{"title":"Finding and using $k$","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$y$ varies directly as $x$, and $y=12$ when $x=4$. (a) Find the equation. (b) Find $y$ when $x=10$. (c) Find $x$ when $y=51$."}],"steps":["(a) $y=kx$: $12=4k$, $k=3$, so $y=3x$.","(b) $y=3\\times10=30$.","(c) $51=3x$, $x=17$."],"answer":"(a) $y=3x$ (b) 30 (c) 17","figs":[]},{"title":"Which variation?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Decide how $y$ varies with $x$ in each table, and find the equation. (a) $x$: 2, 5, 8, 12; $y$: 7, 17.5, 28, 42. (b) $x$: 2, 3, 6, 8; $y$: 24, 16, 8, 6. (c) $x$: 1, 2, 3, 5; $y$: 3, 12, 27, 75."}],"steps":["(a) $\\dfrac yx$: $\\dfrac72=3.5$, $\\dfrac{17.5}{5}=3.5$, $\\dfrac{28}{8}=3.5$, $\\dfrac{42}{12}=3.5$. Constant ratio: $y=3.5x$, direct variation.","(b) $xy$: $48, 48, 48, 48$. Constant product: $y=\\dfrac{48}{x}$, inverse variation.","(c) $\\dfrac yx$: 3, 6, 9, 15, not constant. $\\dfrac{y}{x^2}$: $\\dfrac31=3$, $\\dfrac{12}{4}=3$, $\\dfrac{27}{9}=3$, $\\dfrac{75}{25}=3$. So $y=3x^2$."],"answer":"(a) $y=3.5x$ (b) $y=\\dfrac{48}{x}$ (c) $y=3x^2$","figs":[]},{"title":"Accra to Kumasi","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The time $T$ (hours) to travel from Accra to Kumasi varies inversely as the average speed $S$ (km/h). At 60 km/h the trip takes 4 hours. (a) Find the equation. (b) Find the time at 80 km/h. (c) What average speed is needed to arrive in 2 h 30 min? (d) Why might the model fail during the festive season?"}],"steps":["(a) $T=\\dfrac kS$: $4=\\dfrac{k}{60}$, $k=240$. So $T=\\dfrac{240}{S}$ ($k$ is the distance, 240 km).","(b) $T=\\dfrac{240}{80}=3$ hours.","(c) $2.5=\\dfrac{240}{S}$, so $S=\\dfrac{240}{2.5}=96$ km/h.","(d) The model assumes a constant average speed. Heavy traffic, roadblocks, accidents and long stops at stations make the speed vary and add waiting time, so actual times are longer than predicted."],"answer":"(a) $T=\\dfrac{240}{S}$ (b) 3 h (c) 96 km/h","figs":[]},{"title":"Workers and time","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The time $t$ hours taken to finish a repair job varies inversely as the number of workers $w$. Four workers take 6 hours. (a) How many workers are needed to finish in 2 hours? (b) How long would 5 workers take? (c) Explain why the model cannot hold for 48 workers."}],"steps":["(a) $t=\\dfrac kw$: $6=\\dfrac k4$, $k=24$ (24 worker-hours). For $t=2$: $w=\\dfrac{24}{2}=12$ workers.","(b) $t=\\dfrac{24}{5}=4.8$ hours $=4$ h 48 min.","(c) The model predicts $\\dfrac{24}{48}=0.5$ h, but 48 people cannot all work on one car or machine at once; they would get in each other’s way. The model holds only for a sensible range of $w$."],"answer":"(a) 12 workers (b) 4.8 h (c) too many workers cannot share the work","figs":["w04-workers"]},{"title":"Stopping distance","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The stopping distance $d$ metres of a car varies as the square of its speed $v$ km/h. At 40 km/h, $d=18$ m. (a) Find $d$ at 80 km/h. (b) Find the speed for a stopping distance of 50 m. (c) By what percentage does $d$ increase if the speed increases by 25%?"}],"steps":["$d=kv^2$: $18=k\\times1600$, $k=\\dfrac{18}{1600}=\\dfrac{9}{800}$.","(a) $d=\\dfrac{9}{800}\\times6400=72$ m. (Doubling $v$ multiplies $d$ by $2^2=4$.)","(b) $50=\\dfrac{9}{800}v^2$, $v^2=\\dfrac{40\\,000}{9}$, $v=\\dfrac{200}{3}\\approx66.7$ km/h.","(c) Factor $1.25^2=1.5625$, so $d$ increases by 56.25%."],"answer":"(a) 72 m (b) about 66.7 km/h (c) 56.25%","figs":["w04-stopping"]},{"title":"Light intensity","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The intensity $I$ (lux) of light from a lamp varies inversely as the square of the distance $d$ (m) from the lamp. At 2 m, $I=400$ lux. (a) Find $I$ at 5 m. (b) At what distance is $I=100$ lux? (c) Explain the law using the picture of light spreading out."}],"steps":["$I=\\dfrac{k}{d^2}$: $400=\\dfrac k4$, $k=1600$.","(a) $I=\\dfrac{1600}{25}=64$ lux.","(b) $100=\\dfrac{1600}{d^2}$, $d^2=16$, $d=4$ m.","(c) The same light spreads over an area that grows as $d^2$: at twice the distance it covers 4 times the area, so each square receives $\\tfrac14$ of the light (Figure 4.6)."],"answer":"(a) 64 lux (b) 4 m","figs":["w04-light"]},{"title":"A pendulum","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The period $T$ seconds of a simple pendulum varies as the square root of its length $L$ metres. A 1 m pendulum has period 2 s. (a) Find the period of a 2.25 m pendulum. (b) Find the length for a period of 1 s. (c) How must the length change to double the period?"}],"steps":["$T=k\\sqrt L$: $2=k\\sqrt1$, $k=2$, so $T=2\\sqrt L$.","(a) $T=2\\sqrt{2.25}=2\\times1.5=3$ s.","(b) $1=2\\sqrt L$, $\\sqrt L=0.5$, $L=0.25$ m.","(c) $T\\propto\\sqrt L$, so doubling $T$ needs $\\sqrt L$ doubled, that is $L$ multiplied by $4$."],"answer":"(a) 3 s (b) 0.25 m (c) multiply the length by 4","figs":[]},{"title":"Joint variation","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$y$ varies jointly as $x$ and $z$, and $y=24$ when $x=2$ and $z=3$. (a) Find the equation. (b) Find $y$ when $x=5$ and $z=-2$. (c) Find $z$ when $y=60$ and $x=3$."}],"steps":["(a) $y=kxz$: $24=k\\times2\\times3=6k$, $k=4$. So $y=4xz$.","(b) $y=4\\times5\\times(-2)=-40$.","(c) $60=4\\times3\\times z=12z$, $z=5$."],"answer":"(a) $y=4xz$ (b) $-40$ (c) 5","figs":[]},{"title":"The volume of a cone","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The volume $V$ of a cone varies jointly as its height $h$ and the square of its radius $r$. A cone of radius 6 ft and height 10 ft has volume $120\\pi$ cubic feet. (a) Find $k$. (b) Find the volume of a cone of radius 12 ft and height 2 ft. (c) Check (b) by scaling."}],"steps":["(a) $V=khr^2$: $120\\pi=k\\times10\\times36=360k$, $k=\\dfrac{120\\pi}{360}=\\dfrac{\\pi}{3}$. (This is the familiar $V=\\tfrac13\\pi r^2h$.)","(b) $V=\\dfrac{\\pi}{3}\\times2\\times144=96\\pi\\approx301.6$ ft³.","(c) Radius $\\times2$ gives $\\times4$; height $\\times\\tfrac15$ gives $\\times\\tfrac15$. So $V=120\\pi\\times4\\times\\tfrac15=96\\pi$ ✓."],"answer":"(a) $\\dfrac{\\pi}{3}$ (b) $96\\pi\\approx301.6$ ft³","figs":["w04-cone"]},{"title":"Area of a triangle","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The area $A$ of a triangle varies jointly as its base $b$ and height $h$. $A=30$ cm² when $b=5$ cm and $h=12$ cm. (a) Find $k$. (b) Find $A$ when $b=10$ cm and $h=15$ cm. (c) Show what happens to the area when both base and height are doubled."}],"steps":["(a) $A=kbh$: $30=k\\times5\\times12=60k$, $k=0.5$.","(b) $A=0.5\\times10\\times15=75$ cm².","(c) New area $=0.5\\times(2b)\\times(2h)=4\\times(0.5bh)=4A$: the area is multiplied by **4**."],"answer":"(a) 0.5 (b) 75 cm² (c) the area becomes four times as large","figs":[]},{"title":"Solving problems in teams","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The number of minutes $T$ needed to solve a set of problems varies directly as the number of problems $P$ and inversely as the number of people $N$ working on them. Four people take 36 minutes to solve 18 problems. (a) Find the equation. (b) How long will 8 people take to solve 24 problems? (c) How many people are needed to solve 45 problems in 30 minutes?"}],"steps":["(a) $T=\\dfrac{kP}{N}$: $36=\\dfrac{18k}{4}$, so $18k=144$ and $k=8$. $T=\\dfrac{8P}{N}$.","(b) $T=\\dfrac{8\\times24}{8}=24$ minutes.","(c) $30=\\dfrac{8\\times45}{N}$, $N=\\dfrac{360}{30}=12$ people."],"answer":"(a) $T=\\dfrac{8P}{N}$ (b) 24 min (c) 12 people","figs":[]},{"title":"Gas pressure","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The pressure $P$ of a gas varies jointly as its temperature $T$ and the number of moles $n$, and inversely as its volume $V$. $P=100$ when $n=2$, $T=300$ and $V=10$. (a) Find $k$. (b) Find $P$ when $n=3$, $T=250$ and $V=12$. (c) If $T$ is doubled and $V$ is halved, what happens to $P$?"}],"steps":["(a) $P=\\dfrac{knT}{V}$: $100=\\dfrac{k\\times2\\times300}{10}=60k$, $k=\\dfrac{100}{60}=\\dfrac53$.","(b) $P=\\dfrac53\\times\\dfrac{3\\times250}{12}=\\dfrac{5\\times250}{12}=\\dfrac{1250}{12}\\approx104.17$.","(c) $P$ is multiplied by $\\dfrac{2}{1/2}=4$."],"answer":"(a) $\\dfrac53$ (b) about 104.17 (c) $P$ becomes four times as large","figs":[]},{"title":"Crop yield","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A research team finds that crop yield $Y$ (kg) varies directly as rainfall $R$ (mm) and inversely as temperature $T$ (°C). When $R=100$ and $T=30$, $Y=50$. (a) Find the model and interpret $k$. (b) Predict $Y$ when $R=150$ and $T=25$. (c) Suggest how the model changes if fertiliser adds a fixed 20 kg regardless of rainfall and temperature, and find the new yield for (b)."}],"steps":["(a) $Y=\\dfrac{kR}{T}$: $50=\\dfrac{100k}{30}$, $k=\\dfrac{1500}{100}=15$. So $Y=\\dfrac{15R}{T}$. Here $k$ is the yield (kg) produced per mm of rain when the temperature is 1 °C: it measures how strongly the crop responds to rain.","(b) $Y=\\dfrac{15\\times150}{25}=90$ kg. More rain and a cooler temperature both increase yield, so the prediction is plausible within the tested range; but very heavy rain causes flooding, so the model cannot be used for any $R$.","(c) A fixed addition gives $Y=\\dfrac{15R}{T}+20$ (this is a partial variation, see Week 5). For (b): $90+20=110$ kg."],"answer":"(a) $Y=\\dfrac{15R}{T}$ (b) 90 kg (c) $Y=\\dfrac{15R}{T}+20$; 110 kg","figs":[]},{"title":"Percentage changes","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$z$ varies directly as the square of $x$ and inversely as $y$. Find the percentage change in $z$ when (a) $x$ increases by 10% and $y$ decreases by 20% (b) $x$ decreases by 20% and $y$ increases by 25%."}],"steps":["$z=\\dfrac{kx^2}{y}$, so the factor on $z$ is $\\dfrac{(\\text{factor on }x)^2}{\\text{factor on }y}$.","(a) $\\dfrac{1.1^2}{0.8}=\\dfrac{1.21}{0.8}=1.5125$: $z$ increases by **51.25%**.","(b) $\\dfrac{0.8^2}{1.25}=\\dfrac{0.64}{1.25}=0.512$: $z$ decreases by $100\\%-51.2\\%=$ **48.8%**."],"answer":"(a) increase of 51.25% (b) decrease of 48.8%","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results","items":["Direct: $y=kx$, $\\dfrac yx$ constant, straight line through the origin.","Inverse: $y=\\dfrac kx$, $xy$ constant, hyperbola.","Powers: $y=kx^2$, $y=kx^3$, $y=k\\sqrt x$, $y=\\dfrac{k}{x^2}$ (inverse square).","Joint: $y=kxz$. Combined: $y=\\dfrac{kx}{z}$.","Method: write with $k$ → find $k$ → write the equation → substitute.","Scaling: if $y=\\dfrac{kx^m}{z^n}$, the factor on $y$ is $\\dfrac{(\\text{factor on }x)^m}{(\\text{factor on }z)^n}$."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"Which equation shows that $y$ varies directly as the square of $x$?","options":["$y=kx^2$","$y=kx$","$y=\\dfrac{k}{x^2}$","$y=k\\sqrt x$"],"correct":0,"explain":"Direct variation with $x^2$."},{"q":"$y$ varies directly as $x$ and $y=12$ when $x=4$. When $x=10$, $y=$","options":["30","48","33","22"],"correct":0,"explain":"$k=3$, so $y=30$."},{"q":"Four workers take 6 hours to do a job. (d) If both $L$ and $d$ are doubled, what happens to $R$?","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) $R=\\dfrac{kL}{d^2}$: $0.6=\\dfrac{50k}{4}$, so $k=\\dfrac{2.4}{50}=0.048$. $R=\\dfrac{0.048L}{d^2}$."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) $R=\\dfrac{0.048\\times120}{9}=\\dfrac{5.76}{9}=0.64$ ohms."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) $0.9=\\dfrac{0.048L}{2.25}$, so $L=\\dfrac{0.9\\times2.25}{0.048}=\\dfrac{2.025}{0.048}=42.1875\\approx42.2$ m."},{"k":"p","text":"(d) Factor $\\dfrac{2}{2^2}=\\dfrac12$: the resistance is halved."}]},{"q":"The cost $C$ (GH₵) of feeding students on a trip varies jointly as the number of students $n$ and the number of days $d$. (e) Find the flow rate of one pipe.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) $nt$: $240, 240, 240, 240, 240$. Decrease $=100\\%-44.4\\%=55.6\\%$."}]},{"q":"A canteen operator says: “If the number of students doubles, I need twice as many cooks, twice as much food and twice as much time to serve.” (a) Identify which parts of the claim are reasonable direct variations. (c) Write a model for the serving time $T$ in terms of the number of students $s$ and the number of servers $w$, and test it with $T=40$ minutes for 600 students and 5 servers: find $T$ for 1200 students and 10 servers.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) The amount of food is reasonably proportional to the number of students. The number of cooks may grow roughly in proportion, but not exactly: some tasks (lighting fires, planning) do not grow with numbers."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) Serving time varies directly as the number of students but **inversely** as the number of servers. If the servers are doubled as well, the time does not double."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) $T=\\dfrac{ks}{w}$: $40=\\dfrac{600k}{5}$, $k=\\dfrac{1}{3}$. Such a total is made of:"},{"k":"ul","items":["a **fixed part** (the constant or starting value), and","a **variable part** that changes in direct proportion to another quantity."]},{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Partial variation","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"$y$ is **partly constant and partly varies as $x$** if"},{"k":"math","tex":"y=kx+c\\qquad(c\\neq0),"},{"k":"p","text":"where $c$ is the fixed part and $k$ is the rate of change (the constant of variation of the variable part)."}]},{"k":"p","text":"The graph of $y=kx+c$ is a **straight line** with gradient $k$ and $y$-intercept $c$. (d) Show that the fare does not vary directly as the distance."}],"steps":["(a) $F=2x+8$.","(b) $F=2(15)+8=38$, that is GH₵38.","(c) $2x+8=30$, $2x=22$, $x=11$ km.","(d) 5 km costs $2(5)+8=18$; 10 km costs $28$. Under 4 N it is 22 cm long; under 10 N it is 28 cm long. (a) Find the natural length and the extension per newton. (b) Find the load that gives a length of 30 cm. (c) Which quantity varies directly as the load?"}],"steps":["(a) $L=kF+L_0$: $22=4k+L_0$, $28=10k+L_0$. Subtract: $6k=6$, $k=1$ cm/N. Then $L_0=18$ cm.","(b) $F+18=30$, $F=12$ N.","(c) The **extension** $L-L_0=F$ varies directly as the load (Hooke’s law); the **length** is a partial variation."],"answer":"(a) 18 cm; 1 cm per newton (b) 12 N (c) the extension","figs":[]},{"title":"Temperature scales","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The Fahrenheit temperature $F$ is partly constant and partly varies as the Celsius temperature $C$. Water freezes at $0^\\circ$C $=32^\\circ$F and boils at $100^\\circ$C $=212^\\circ$F. (a) Find the equation. (b) Convert normal body temperature $37^\\circ$C. (c) At what temperature do the two scales give the same reading?"}],"steps":["(a) $F=kC+c$: $c=32$ from $(0,32)$; $212=100k+32$, $k=1.8$. So $F=1.8C+32$.","(b) $F=1.8(37)+32=66.6+32=98.6^\\circ$F.","(c) $C=1.8C+32$, $-0.8C=32$, $C=-40$. So $-40^\\circ$C $=-40^\\circ$F."],"answer":"(a) $F=1.8C+32$ (b) $98.6^\\circ$F (c) $-40^\\circ$","figs":[]},{"title":"Partly constant, partly as the square","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"$y$ is partly constant and partly varies as $x^2$. When $x=2$, $y=14$, and when $x=4$, $y=38$. (a) Find the relationship. (b) Find $y$ when $x=5$. (c) Find $x$ when $y=78$."}],"steps":["(a) $y=a+bx^2$: $14=a+4b$ and $38=a+16b$. Subtract: $12b=24$, $b=2$; then $a=14-8=6$. So $y=6+2x^2$.","(b) $y=6+2(25)=56$.","(c) $6+2x^2=78$, $x^2=36$, $x=\\pm6$."],"answer":"(a) $y=6+2x^2$ (b) 56 (c) $x=\\pm6$","figs":[]},{"title":"Sharing a bus","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The cost $C$ (GH₵) per student of an excursion is partly constant (food) and partly varies inversely as the number of students $n$ (the bus hire is shared). For 20 students $C=95$; for 50 students $C=62$. (a) Find the relationship and interpret the constants. (b) Find the cost per student for 40 students. (c) What is the least number of students for the cost to be at most GH₵60?"}],"steps":["(a) $C=a+\\dfrac bn$: $95=a+\\dfrac{b}{20}$, $62=a+\\dfrac{b}{50}$.","Subtract: $33=b\\left(\\dfrac{1}{20}-\\dfrac{1}{50}\\right)=\\dfrac{3b}{100}$, so $b=1100$. Then $a=95-55=40$.","$C=40+\\dfrac{1100}{n}$: GH₵40 is the food per student and GH₵1100 is the bus hire.","(b) $C=40+\\dfrac{1100}{40}=40+27.5=67.5$, that is GH₵67.50.","(c) $40+\\dfrac{1100}{n}\\le60$ gives $\\dfrac{1100}{n}\\le20$, $n\\ge55$: at least 55 students."],"answer":"(a) $C=40+\\dfrac{1100}{n}$ (b) GH₵67.50 (c) 55","figs":["w05-excursion"]},{"title":"Thinking and braking distances","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The stopping distance $d$ m of a car is the sum of the thinking distance, which varies as the speed $v$ km/h, and the braking distance, which varies as $v^2$. At 40 km/h, $d=16$ m; at 80 km/h, $d=48$ m. (a) Find the relationship. (b) Find $d$ at 100 km/h. (c) What fraction of the stopping distance at 100 km/h is braking?"}],"steps":["(a) $d=av+bv^2$: $16=40a+1600b$ and $48=80a+6400b$.","Doubling the first: $32=80a+3200b$. Subtract from the second: $16=3200b$, $b=0.005$. Then $40a=16-8=8$, $a=0.2$.","$d=0.2v+0.005v^2$.","(b) $d=0.2(100)+0.005(10\\,000)=20+50=70$ m.","(c) $\\dfrac{50}{70}=\\dfrac57\\approx71\\%$."],"answer":"(a) $d=0.2v+0.005v^2$ (b) 70 m (c) $\\dfrac57$","figs":["w05-stopping"]},{"title":"A bakery’s break-even","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A bakery’s daily cost is GH₵150 (rent, wages, fuel) plus GH₵2.50 for each loaf baked. Each loaf sells for GH₵4. (a) Write the cost $C$ and the income $I$ for $n$ loaves. (b) Find the break-even number of loaves. (c) Find the profit when 240 loaves are sold. (d) How many loaves give a daily profit of GH₵300?"}],"steps":["(a) $C=150+2.5n$ (partial variation); $I=4n$ (direct variation).","(b) $4n=150+2.5n$, $1.5n=150$, $n=100$ loaves.","(c) Profit $=I-C=4n-150-2.5n=1.5n-150$. For $n=240$: $360-150=210$, that is GH₵210.","(d) $1.5n-150=300$, $n=300$ loaves."],"answer":"(b) 100 loaves (c) GH₵210 (d) 300 loaves","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results","items":["Partial variation: $y=kx+c$ with $c\\neq0$; straight line with gradient $k$ and intercept $c$, not through the origin.","From two points: $k=\\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$, then $c=y_1-kx_1$.","Doubling $x$ does **not** double $y$; only the variable part doubles.","Break-even of $k_1x+c_1$ and $k_2x+c_2$: $x=\\dfrac{c_2-c_1}{k_1-k_2}$.","Extended forms: $y=a+bx^2$, $y=a+\\dfrac bx$, $y=ax+bx^2$; use two points and solve simultaneously."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"Which equation is a partial variation?","options":["$y=4x+7$","$y=4x$","$y=\\dfrac4x$","$y=4x^2$"],"correct":0,"explain":"It has a fixed part, 7, and a part varying as $x$."},{"q":"The graph of $y=3x+5$ meets the $y$-axis at","options":["$(0,5)$","$(0,3)$","$(5,0)$","$(0,0)$"],"correct":0,"explain":"The intercept is the fixed part."},{"q":"A taxi charges GH₵6 plus GH₵3 per km. Then $b=$","options":["1.5","2","6","3"],"correct":0,"explain":"$8b=12$."},{"q":"For $y=kx+c$ ($c\\neq0$), doubling $x$","options":["does not double $y$","doubles $y$","halves $y$","leaves $y$ unchanged"],"correct":0,"explain":"Only the $kx$ part doubles."},{"q":"$C=40+\\dfrac{1100}{n}$. As $n$ becomes very large, $C$ approaches","options":["40","0","1100","1140"],"correct":0,"explain":"$\\dfrac{1100}{n}\\to0$."},{"q":"A spring is 15 cm long with no load and stretches 2 cm per newton. Its length under 6 N is","options":["27 cm","12 cm","17 cm","30 cm"],"correct":0,"explain":"$15+2\\times6=27$."}],"exercise":[{"q":"An electricity bill is a service charge of GH₵12 plus GH₵1.60 per kWh. (d) Another firm charges GH₵75 per day with no fixed charge. For how many days is the other firm cheaper?","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) Each extra day adds GH₵60 ($210-150$, $270-210$, and $\\tfrac{390-270}{2}=60$): a constant rate. But $\\dfrac Cd$ is 150, 105, 90, 78, not constant. So $C$ is partly constant and partly varies as $d$."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) $C=60d+90$: GH₵60 is the daily charge and GH₵90 is a fixed charge (delivery and setting up)."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) The graph is a straight line from $(0,90)$ through $(5,390)$; at $d=4.5$, $C=60(4.5)+90=360$."},{"k":"p","text":"(d) $75d<60d+90$ gives $15d<90$, $d<6$. The other firm is cheaper for hires of 1 to 5 days; at 6 days the costs are equal (GH₵450)."}]},{"q":"A school prints its terminal reports. (d) Explain in terms of gradients and intercepts why the cheaper printer changes.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) $A=120+1.2n$, $B=300+0.75n$."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) $120+1.2n=300+0.75n$ gives $0.45n=180$, $n=400$ reports."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) $A=120+1800=1920$; $B=300+1125=1425$. Choose B; saving GH₵495."},{"k":"p","text":"(d) A has the smaller intercept (lower setup) so it is cheaper for small orders; B has the smaller gradient (lower cost per report) so its line rises more slowly and is below A’s line after the crossing point at 400 reports."}]},{"q":"The cost $C$ of producing $n$ exercise books is partly constant and partly varies as $n$.
